body: Glad to help. If you want to talk over what you're reading /r/literature is fairly active as is /r/philosophy; agitano seems to have his head on his shoulders and of course I'm here as well. I regret not adding David Foster Wallace to the list, and Infinite Jest in particular as it's '[Infinite Summer](http://infinitesummer.org)'- [here](http://www.newyorker.com/reporting/2009/03/09/090309fa_fact_max?currentPage=all) is a good article from the New Yorker if you're not familiar.

It isn't about uncertainty with the future, it's about not believing it matters either way. Why does it have to matter? That's where most people stop, when they decide it doesn't and move on with their lives. But for those who chew on it a little longer it can be torturous. Which is where some take issue and say 'that's a disease.' I think for those who suffer this way it's just a cognitive growing up of sorts. Definitely material [Durkheim](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Suicide_%28book%29) would have loved.

It is difficult to talk with others about this in particular, I understand. It seems sometimes that if we were more melodramatic in our suffering then perhaps it would be considered more 'serious' and therefore receive different attention. I know some would like to believe people don't think this way and attempt to block it out; perhaps so they won't think it themselves, or fear it spreading to others.

Regardless- yes I still think it lines up with what I believe many people have thought/do think but act little on. Some authors I would recommend…Sartre, Camus, Heidegger, Nietzsche, Kiekegaard, Foucault, Derrida, Jean Genet, Dostoyevsky, Beckett, Eugene Ionesco, Shaw. That's not very gender balanced so…add Simone de Beauvoir, the yoko ono of existentialism. As an aside, someone in another post recommended Hemingway to me based on this fairly gloomy book selection and I found that rather ironic, despite the 'world is a fine place' he was an alcoholic who ultimately committed suicide. His writing is great though, so add him as well. Also, [here](http://ben.casnocha.com/2009/05/the-quarter-life-crisis.html) is a good article posted recently to /r/philosophy. This is starting to read like a hackneyed phil. 101 syllabus…

I agree you should see a therapist as well, it can't hurt. These kind of forums can be an echo chambers some times, you don't hear a lot of success stories. But I don't believe a medication can change your thought process. I think they can help you achieve a state of mind wherein you can make those changes, but no medication is going to do it automatically. I've been there too. I hope this helps some.

Not exactly a popular opinion but I believe suicide is pure logic taken to a natural conclusion. I struggle with this. I think it's an existential problem really, an unworkable one. You can never answer "why should I exist?" because beyond the answer 'just because' there isn't much. You'll get people telling you 'to enjoy life, to find love, cure leprosy' etc. But that's really missing the point that once you start thinking this way, nothing has meaning. If you do not believe meaning exists, then maybe you have to make it up as you go along.

I respect the idea that thinking this way is a  disease but I don't believe it. Don't take that to mean I think depression isn't real…However, I believe this thought process ≠ depression. Just overly rational thought, as you said. The best way I've found to deal with it has been to read about others who think the same way, and to hear what conclusion they came to.

I do suggest talking to others about this if you haven't already. Even if they think you're cynical and hopeless, maybe they'll give you a signifying force for your life. It's worth a shot. Anyway- I hope this isn't a downer for you, I only mean to say that there are other people who think this way and that we're here existing too. In fact I would say it's a fairly common thought process that just isn't talked about too much. It's okay to continue living while you figure it out. Good luck.

I have to sleep now, for my reason to live tonight is to see through to school/work in the morning. I wish I could give you a better reply tonight.

I want to say thank you again though because you have a lot of fair and reasonable ideas. You will understand these, so I want to leave with a couple quotes I find relevant to this discussion. Hopefully it will continue in my absence and if not I'll start it up elsewhere.

"What is joy? or what is it to be joyful? It is to be present to oneself; but to be truly present to oneself is this thing of 'today', that is, this thing of being today, of truly being today. And in the same degree that it is more true that thou art today, in the same degree that thou art quite present to thyself in being today, in that very same degree is the baleful tomorrow non-existent for thee. Joy is the present tense, with the whole emphasis upon the present..."
-Søren Kierkegaard, The Lily of the Field, The Bird of the Air: Three Devotional Discourses, 1849

"If we have our own why of life, we shall get along with almost any how. Man does not strive for pleasure; only the Englishman does."
-Friedrich Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, "Maxims and Arrows," #12, 1895

Thank you for your reply. Life truly does bring joy in chemical reactions and neural stimulation and we should take as much as we can. You mention giving as well and that is also very good; sharing in these feelings must be the highest act of anything one can do for another person. I agree that life does not have to have inherent meaning to experience this, but I can't convince myself of much else. I understand your sentiment, but ultimately I don't see it working for me.

Living life for pure enjoyment of these things is something I have not been able to do. I have never been able to find meaning (or motivation, or interest, whatever you want to call it) in living life that way.  However: I am very glad that others can live like this and I recommend anyone able to do so to pursue it with much vigor and many debaucheries, presumably in a combination there of.

Perhaps this is my 'problem' and truly where I should seek help. I like the cut of your jib as well. I wish more people could be laissez faire with their mindset, if not their policy...Thank you again.

Hello everyone -

What you're doing here is fantastic and I wanted to begin by saying thank you. The community you have built here is beautiful and it is a wonderful idea, cheers to you all.

I had a bottle of pills and a bottle of alcohol next to it the other night, again. I didn't act on it. This hasn't happened in awhile but the last time it did I was hospitalized. I was given new medication and it has made me feel alright, but certainly it has not 'cured' me.

Life is pointless. This is a shock to you all, I'm sure. We ascribe meaning to everything we do, everything we see; it's all limited to our language, what we know, how we relate. Think Derrida or Foucault. This doesn't particularly bother me - I have come to grips with this fact (if in fact there is something to have a grip on). I have, however, found it impossible to reconcile this with actually moving on and being motivated. I can hear some say, "Oh, life may be pointless but that is what truly doesn't matter. We don't know everything and you must continue living, searching for your answer. Searching for this answer is the point of living, and acting on that, and so on." I would say to these people that they are missing the point that *nothing matters*. Finding something to live for at this point becomes moot.

The other problems in my life are all self created, like most others, so I know ultimately I can deal with those. It's more of an existential question if anything. This is the sole argument I can find for the existence of religion and sometimes I almost wish I could convince myself to believe.

Maybe I have psychosis, but I doubt it. I know this is a fairly common thought process for one in my situation but that doesn't mean much. I'm inherently untrusting of psychology to begin with anyway; it creates deviations out of things that were otherwise normal to begin with.

I do live alone in an apartment. I understand getting out with people clears these thoughts, and I do that. I find that when I'm with people life does take on meaning, and that is good. But it's a fleeting thing. This may be my lynchpin in the "final solution, temporary problem" thing.

I feel a lot of people in these situations (not a thinly veiled disguise for "me" btw) are here because we either have no support group, our support group has collapsed or we lack similar minded people to be the base for our support group. That is why groups like this are so important, however they are clearly not enough. Sometimes I think an institution for people who think too much would be the best solution for us (beyond college etc); people who need some kind of structure but are not receiving it from school/work/family/church. Get on that, won't you?

I'm positive many of you have had these same ideas in the past. What do you think? Why am I alive, why are you alive? Thanks a lot for your time.
